title: Society of Mind and Multi-Agent Debate

questions.question: Several agents independently answer a problem, then compare reasoning and revise. What added operation distinguishes debate from one-shot voting?
options: The system discards every answer before counting votes
Agents read peers' answers and update across rounds
A single model samples one completion at temperature zero
A judge chooses a tool without seeing any answers
questions.explanation: Debate adds an exchange step: agents inspect peer answers, critique them, and may revise over rounds before aggregation. Discarding every answer before counting would leave nothing to compare; it removes rather than adds cross-agent information.

questions.question: What do the lesson's ablations say about the two debate design knobs?
options: Only one agent matters; rounds add no information
Both agent count and exchange rounds contribute independently
Neither knob matters once a majority is reached
Only more rounds matter; agent count makes no difference
questions.explanation: The ablations treat agent count and debate rounds as separate contributors: increasing participants and allowing exchange both add signal. “Only more rounds” overlooks the measured benefit of adding agents.

questions.question: Why can a heterogeneous debate reduce monoculture errors?
options: Different models can share fewer correlated errors
A weaker model always improves the final consensus
Different models guarantee every answer is correct
Model diversity removes the need to verify results
questions.explanation: Different base models can have less-correlated failure patterns, making an ensemble less vulnerable to one shared hallucination. Diversity is not a correctness guarantee; the option promising every answer is right overstates what decorrelation provides.

questions.question: A debate's agents begin repeating the most confident speaker's answer without checking it. Which failure mode is this?
options: Task starvation
Schema drift
Sycophancy cascade
Memory overflow
questions.explanation: A sycophancy cascade is social influence: agents copy a confident peer instead of independently checking the claim. Memory overflow is a context-capacity issue and does not describe the observed deference.

questions.question: All agents agree after several rounds. What conclusion is justified by agreement alone?
options: The group no longer needs a verifier
The model family has eliminated correlated errors
The answer is true because every agent converged
Consensus alone does not establish correctness
questions.explanation: Agreement only shows that agents converged on the same response; correlated models or conformity can align them around a false claim. A high agreement rate is therefore not an external proof of the answer.

questions.question: The original question disappears from a long debate, and agents begin discussing a related issue. What mitigation matches the lesson?
options: Allow additional rounds without a stopping rule
Hide earlier messages from the final majority vote
Re-inject the original question in each round
Increase the agent count until a specialist notices
questions.explanation: Re-injecting the original question each round anchors the exchange to the requested task, while a round limit prevents the conversation from drifting indefinitely. Adding rounds without an anchor makes the drift risk worse.
